input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-351: Data Communications and Networks. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course is an in-depth study of data communications and networks. The course covers design of, and algorithms and protocols used in, the physical, data link, network, transport, and application layers in the Internet; methods for modeling and analyzing networks, including graphs, graph algorithms, and discrete event simulation; and an introduction to network science. Programming projects will be required. Pre-requisites: CSCI-251 and (MATH-251 or STAT-251 or STAT-205) or equivalent courses. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have taken CSCI-651. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall

Source excerpts:

[rfc-1122]
Internet hosts implement layered link, internet, transport, and application functions. The link layer moves frames across a directly connected network. IP provides best-effort datagram delivery across interconnected networks. An IP address identifies an interface for internet-layer delivery. Routing selects a next hop toward a destination. Transport protocols add endpoint communication functions above IP. Application protocols define the meaning of exchanged data. Correct analysis distinguishes addresses, routes, packets, frames, sockets, and end-to-end state.

[rfc-9293]
TCP provides a reliable, ordered byte stream between endpoints. Sequence numbers identify positions in that byte stream. Acknowledgments report which data has been received. Retransmission recovers data that is presumed lost. Flow control prevents a sender from exceeding the receiver's advertised capacity. A TCP connection moves through defined protocol states. Connection establishment synchronizes endpoint state before application data transfer. Packet loss, duplication, reordering, delay, and endpoint failure must be separated when reasoning about behavior and performance.

[rit-csci-351]
This course is an in-depth study of data communications and networks. The course covers design of, and algorithms and protocols used in, the physical, data link, network, transport, and application layers in the Internet; methods for modeling and analyzing networks, including graphs, graph algorithms, and discrete event simulation; and an introduction to network science. Programming projects will be required. Pre-requisites: CSCI-251 and (MATH-251 or STAT-251 or STAT-205) or equivalent courses. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have taken CSCI-651. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall

beats.claim: Internet hosts implement layered link, internet, transport, and application functions, with each layer handling distinct data units and responsibilities.
beats.example: A packet traverses from the application layer down to the physical layer, where each layer adds headers and encapsulates the payload.
beats.title: Layered Architecture Overview
beats.visualDirection: Display a vertical stack diagram with labeled layers (Application, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical) and show a packet being encapsulated layer by layer.

beats.claim: The link layer moves frames across a directly connected network, while the physical layer handles the transmission of bits over a medium.
beats.example: Ethernet frames are transmitted over copper or fiber optic cables, with the physical layer managing signal integrity and the data link layer handling addressing and error detection.
beats.title: Physical and Data Link Layers
beats.visualDirection: Show a side-by-side comparison of a physical layer signal waveform and a data link layer frame structure with MAC addresses and CRC.

beats.claim: IP provides best-effort datagram delivery across interconnected networks, and an IP address identifies an interface for internet-layer delivery.
beats.example: IPv4 addresses like 192.168.1.10 assign a unique identifier to a network interface, enabling routers to forward packets toward a destination.
beats.title: Network Layer and IP Addressing
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a router table with source/destination IP addresses and next-hop destinations, highlighting how IP addresses map to interfaces.

beats.claim: Routing selects a next hop toward a destination, using algorithms to determine the most efficient path through interconnected networks.
beats.example: OSPF or BGP algorithms evaluate link costs and topology to compute shortest paths, updating routing tables dynamically.
beats.title: Routing and Path Selection
beats.visualDirection: Render a network graph with nodes and weighted edges, showing a routing algorithm tracing a path from source to destination.

beats.claim: Transport protocols add endpoint communication functions above IP, with TCP providing a reliable, ordered byte stream between endpoints.
beats.example: Web browsing uses TCP to ensure that HTML chunks arrive in the correct sequence without gaps or duplicates.
beats.title: Transport Layer and TCP Basics
beats.visualDirection: Draw a TCP handshake sequence (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) with labeled sequence numbers and state transitions.

beats.claim: A TCP connection moves through defined protocol states, and sequence numbers identify positions in that byte stream while acknowledgments report received data.
beats.example: When a packet is lost, TCP detects the gap via missing acknowledgments and triggers retransmission to recover the missing data.
beats.title: TCP State Machine and Reliability
beats.visualDirection: Display a state diagram showing TCP connection states (CLOSED, LISTEN, ESTABLISHED, FIN_WAIT, etc.) with transition triggers.

beats.claim: Flow control prevents a sender from exceeding the receiver's advertised capacity, ensuring stable data transfer rates.
beats.example: The sliding window mechanism in TCP adjusts the send window size based on receiver acknowledgments to avoid overwhelming the network.
beats.title: Flow Control and Congestion Management
beats.visualDirection: Animate a sender and receiver with a sliding window, showing how the window shrinks or expands based on ACK feedback.

beats.claim: Methods for modeling and analyzing networks include graphs, graph algorithms, and discrete event simulation, enabling systematic performance evaluation.
beats.example: Representing routers as nodes and links as edges allows Dijkstra's algorithm to compute minimum-cost paths for packet routing.
beats.title: Network Modeling with Graphs
beats.visualDirection: Show a network graph with labeled nodes, edges, and weights, alongside a step-by-step visualization of Dijkstra's algorithm exploring paths.

beats.claim: Discrete event simulation models network behavior by tracking individual packets and events, providing accurate performance metrics without continuous monitoring.
beats.example: Simulating packet arrivals, processing delays, and queueing times helps identify bottlenecks and optimize routing policies.
beats.title: Discrete Event Simulation and Analysis
beats.visualDirection: Present a timeline with discrete events (packet arrival, transmission start, completion, loss) and corresponding queue lengths at routers.

beats.claim: Correct analysis distinguishes addresses, routes, packets, frames, sockets, and end-to-end state, enabling systematic troubleshooting and protocol verification.
beats.example: When a connection fails, verify IP addresses, check routing tables, inspect TCP state transitions, and review frame integrity to isolate the issue.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: List a checklist with checkboxes for: IP address validation, route table inspection, TCP state verification, frame CRC check, and socket configuration review.

learningObjectives: Define and distinguish the five Internet protocol layers (physical, data link, network, transport, application) and their respective responsibilities.
Explain how TCP establishes a reliable, ordered byte stream using sequence numbers, acknowledgments, and state transitions.
Apply graph-based modeling and discrete event simulation concepts to analyze network routing and packet flow.
